rationale: Leviticus 19:17 says "Directly rebuke your neighbor" (BSB), and Matthew 18:15 says "go and confront him privately" (BSB). The English verbs differ, but in Greek the Septuagint of Leviticus 19:17 (Swete) reads ἐλεγμῷ ἐλέγξεις τὸν πλησίον σου, after οὐ μισήσεις τὸν ἀδελφόν σου (not hating "your brother," as the BSB renders it) in 19:17a, and Matthew 18:15 reads ἔλεγξον αὐτὸν in every edition Bible Hub lists: the same verb. Three commentators on Matthew 18:15 draw the line back to Leviticus. The Cambridge Bible notes that "the same Greek word is translated rebuke" there; Ellicott writes that "the substance of the precept is taken from the passage in Leviticus (Leviticus 19:17-18)"; Barnes writes, "This was required under the law, Leviticus 19:17." What the two texts share is one verb and one situation, a brother or neighbor who has done wrong; Matthew names no source. So the type is allusion and the label plausible, as with conn-matt16-leaven-exodus12, where commentators trace a background that Matthew does not cite.
